title: Nitrogen Metabolism: Amino Acids and Nucleotides
summary: Track nitrogen from dietary protein to urea, neurotransmitters and the building blocks of DNA.

lessons.title: Transamination, Deamination and Nitrogen Disposal

levels.kid:
Your body uses protein from food like a big box of building blocks. Each block is an amino acid. Every amino acid carries a special piece that contains **nitrogen**.

When your body has more blocks than it needs, it takes them apart. It can burn the leftover part for energy. But the nitrogen piece is tricky. Loose nitrogen turns into **ammonia**, which is harmful, especially to the brain.

So your body plays pass-the-parcel. Helpers called **enzymes** hand the nitrogen piece from one molecule to another until it reaches the **liver**. The liver packs it safely into **urea**. Urea travels in your blood to your kidneys, and you pee it out.

It is like a recycling team that sorts out the dangerous bits and sends them away safely.
levels.hs:
Proteins are made of **amino acids**, and every amino acid has an **amino group** (-NH2) that contains nitrogen. Your body reuses amino acids to build new proteins. Extras cannot be stored, so they are broken down. The carbon skeleton is burned for energy or turned into glucose or fat. The nitrogen has to be removed safely.

Two key steps do this:
- **Transamination**: an enzyme moves the amino group from an amino acid onto a molecule called **alpha-ketoglutarate**, which becomes the amino acid **glutamate**. The original amino acid becomes a **keto acid** (its carbon skeleton). These enzymes are called **aminotransferases** (or transaminases). They need a helper made from **vitamin B6**.
- **Deamination**: in the liver, glutamate releases its amino group as free **ammonia** (NH3/NH4+).

Ammonia is toxic, particularly to the brain, so the liver quickly turns it into **urea** in the urea cycle. Urea is harmless, dissolves in water, and leaves in urine.

Tissues outside the liver send nitrogen there in safe "carrier" forms. Most tissues use **glutamine**. Muscle mainly uses **alanine**.

Real example: doctors measure two aminotransferases, **ALT** and **AST**, in blood tests. When liver cells are damaged, for instance in hepatitis, these enzymes leak into the blood and their levels rise.
levels.college:
Amino acid catabolism separates two problems: disposing of the **alpha-amino nitrogen** and using the **carbon skeleton**. The nitrogen is funneled through a few key molecules.

**Transamination.** Aminotransferases transfer the amino group of an amino acid to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate and the corresponding alpha-keto acid:
- Alanine + alpha-KG ⇌ pyruvate + glutamate (**ALT**)
- Aspartate + alpha-KG ⇌ oxaloacetate + glutamate (**AST**)

The reactions are freely reversible, with an equilibrium constant near 1, so the same enzymes also make nonessential amino acids. All aminotransferases use **pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)**, derived from vitamin B6. Lysine and threonine are the main exceptions that do not undergo standard transamination.

**Oxidative deamination.** In liver mitochondria, **glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH)** converts glutamate to alpha-KG + NH4+, using NAD+ or NADP+. This makes glutamate the collecting point for nitrogen. GDH is allosterically activated by **ADP** and **GTP**-inhibited, linking nitrogen release to the cell's energy state. Leucine also activates GDH.

**Other ammonia sources**: glutaminase, serine/threonine dehydratases (PLP-dependent), the purine nucleotide cycle in muscle, and gut bacteria that make ammonia absorbed via the portal vein.

**Interorgan transport.**
- **Glutamine synthetase** (ATP-dependent) adds NH4+ to glutamate in most tissues. Glutamine is the major nontoxic blood nitrogen carrier. In liver and kidney, glutaminase releases the ammonia again.
- **Glucose-alanine cycle**: muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine. The liver converts alanine back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and sends glucose back to muscle.

**Fate in the liver.** NH4+ and aspartate (made by AST) supply the two nitrogens of urea. The kidney excretes some NH4+ directly, which also helps acid-base balance.

Carbon skeletons are classed as **glucogenic** (yielding pyruvate or TCA intermediates) or **ketogenic** (yielding acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate). Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
levels.phd:
**PLP chemistry.** In aminotransferases, PLP is bound as an internal aldimine (Schiff base) to an active-site lysine. The incoming amino acid displaces it, forming an external aldimine. Base abstraction of the alpha-hydrogen gives a quinonoid intermediate stabilized by the pyridinium ring acting as an electron sink. Reprotonation at C4' and hydrolysis release the alpha-keto acid and leave **pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP)**. A second keto acid then binds and the steps run in reverse. Kinetically this is a **ping-pong (double-displacement) Bi Bi** mechanism, and it is the textbook case of that pattern. Dunathan's hypothesis explains reaction specificity: the PLP-enzyme orients the bond to be broken perpendicular to the pyridine ring plane, maximizing overlap with the pi system. The same cofactor can therefore catalyze transamination, decarboxylation, or racemization depending on geometry.

**Thermodynamic logic.** Transamination is near-equilibrium, so flux follows substrate supply. The committed disposal steps are GDH, glutamine synthetase, and above all **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I**, which is activated by N-acetylglutamate. GDH flux direction in vivo is debated. Its Km for NH4+ is high, so it probably runs mainly in the deaminating direction in liver. **SIRT4** ADP-ribosylates and inhibits GDH, linking the enzyme to nutrient signaling.

**Liver zonation.** Häussinger's work showed metabolic zoning in the liver lobule. Periportal hepatocytes hold high glutaminase and urea cycle capacity, a high-capacity, low-affinity system. A thin rim of perivenous hepatocytes expresses glutamine synthetase, a low-capacity, high-affinity scavenger that captures ammonia escaping the periportal zone. This arrangement also couples nitrogen disposal to pH, because urea synthesis consumes bicarbonate.

**Branched-chain amino acids** (leucine, isoleucine, valine) are transaminated mainly in muscle by BCAT2. The liver has little BCAT activity. Their keto acids are oxidatively decarboxylated by the **BCKDH complex**, which is regulated by phosphorylation (BCKDK kinase, PPM1K phosphatase). The amino group is exported as alanine and glutamine.

**Renal ammoniagenesis.** In acidosis, proximal tubule glutaminase and PEPCK are upregulated. NH4+ is excreted and new bicarbonate is generated, making glutamine metabolism a pillar of acid-base control.
levels.expert:
**Aminotransferases as biomarkers.** ALT is largely cytosolic and liver-predominant. AST has cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms and is abundant in muscle, heart, and red cells. An AST:ALT ratio above about 2 suggests alcohol-associated liver disease, partly because alcohol depletes PLP and ALT is more PLP-sensitive. Pitfalls:
- Rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise, or hemolysis raise AST, and sometimes ALT, without liver injury.
- B6 deficiency, as in dialysis patients, can falsely lower measured activity if assays lack added PLP.
- Macro-AST, an enzyme bound to immunoglobulin, causes isolated persistent elevation.
- Normal ALT does not exclude cirrhosis.

**GDH gain-of-function.** Activating mutations in GLUD1 that impair GTP inhibition cause **hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia (HI/HA) syndrome**. In beta cells, excess glutamate oxidation raises ATP and drives insulin secretion, especially after protein meals because leucine activates GDH. Patients have hypoglycemia with mild, persistent, usually asymptomatic hyperammonemia, and are often treated with diazoxide. It shows how a disposal enzyme doubles as a fuel sensor.

**Glutamine synthetase and the brain.** Astrocytes are the brain's main ammonia sink. In liver failure, astrocytic glutamine accumulates and acts as an osmolyte and possible mitochondrial "Trojan horse," contributing to astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema. This underlies **hepatic encephalopathy**. Therapies that target gut ammonia production or alternative disposal routes belong to the next lesson. Congenital glutamine synthetase deficiency is rare and causes severe brain malformation.

**Pharmacology hooks.** Isoniazid forms hydrazones with pyridoxal, and the resulting B6 depletion causes neuropathy, which is why pyridoxine is coadministered. **Vigabatrin** irreversibly inactivates the PLP-dependent GABA transaminase (GABA-T). Cycloserine and penicillamine also interfere with PLP. Valproate can raise ammonia, partly by inhibiting carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I through N-acetylglutamate depletion.

**Oncology and frontiers.** Many tumors are "glutamine addicted" and use glutaminase to feed the TCA cycle (anaplerosis). The GLS1 inhibitor telaglenastat (CB-839) showed limited benefit in trials, a reminder of tumor metabolic plasticity. Elevated circulating BCAAs are associated with insulin resistance, and BCKDK inhibitors are in development. An open question is how much ammonia tumors and other tissues recycle into biosynthesis rather than simply dispose of.

keyPoints: Excess amino acids are broken down: carbon skeletons yield energy, nitrogen must be removed
Aminotransferases move amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate (PLP/B6-dependent)
Glutamate dehydrogenase releases free ammonia in liver mitochondria
Glutamine (most tissues) and alanine (muscle) carry nitrogen safely to the liver
The liver converts toxic ammonia to urea, which the kidneys excrete
ALT and AST in blood are markers of liver (and muscle) cell injury

test.q: In a typical transamination, which molecule accepts the amino group?
choices: Urea, forming citrulline in the urea cycle
test.explain: Most aminotransferases transfer the amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate.

test.q: Which cofactor do all aminotransferases require?
test.explain: PLP, derived from vitamin B6, carries the amino group during transamination. Thiamine and biotin serve other enzymes.

test.q: Which enzyme releases free ammonia from glutamate in the liver?
test.explain: Glutamate dehydrogenase carries out oxidative deamination, producing alpha-ketoglutarate and NH4+. Glutamine synthetase does the reverse job of capturing ammonia.

test.q: What is the main nontoxic carrier of nitrogen in the blood from most tissues?
test.explain: Glutamine synthetase packages ammonia into glutamine for safe transport. Urea is the final excreted product, not the carrier.

test.q: Muscle sends nitrogen to the liver mainly as alanine. This is part of the:
test.explain: Muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine. The liver uses the alanine carbon for gluconeogenesis and sends glucose back. The Cori cycle shuttles lactate, not nitrogen.

test.q: ALT transaminates alanine into which keto acid?
test.explain: Alanine plus alpha-KG gives pyruvate plus glutamate. Aspartate yields oxaloacetate through AST.

test.q: Why is free ammonia rapidly converted rather than left in the blood?
choices: It is too large to enter the kidneys
It blocks the liver from storing fat
It is toxic, especially to the brain
test.explain: Ammonia is toxic to the nervous system, so the liver converts it into harmless urea.

test.q: A blood test shows high ALT and AST. The most likely meaning is:
choices: Too much urea in the urine
test.explain: Aminotransferases leak from injured liver cells, for example in hepatitis. Muscle injury can also raise AST.

test.q: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
test.explain: ADP signals low energy and activates GDH, while GTP inhibits it, linking amino acid breakdown to energy need.

test.q: Amino acids whose carbon skeletons yield acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate are called ___.
test.explain: Ketogenic skeletons form ketone body precursors. Glucogenic ones can make glucose.

test.q: What harmless nitrogen-containing compound does the liver make from ammonia for excretion in urine?
test.explain: Urea is water-soluble and nontoxic, and the kidneys excrete it.

test.q: Aminotransferases are also called ___.
test.explain: Transaminase is the older, common name for aminotransferase.

kidTest.q: What are proteins made of?
kidTest.explain: Amino acids are the building blocks of protein.

kidTest.q: What can loose nitrogen turn into?
kidTest.explain: Loose nitrogen becomes ammonia, which is harmful.

kidTest.q: Which organ packs nitrogen into urea?
kidTest.explain: The liver makes urea.

kidTest.q: How does urea leave your body?
kidTest.explain: The kidneys put urea into urine.

kidTest.q: Too much ammonia is harmful to this organ in your head: b _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Ammonia is especially harmful to the brain, so the body clears it quickly.

advancedTest.q: Aminotransferases show ping-pong kinetics because:
choices: The enzyme alternates between two separate active sites on each subunit
Allosteric ADP binding switches the enzyme between two different states
The first product leaves as PLP becomes PMP, before the second substrate binds
Both substrates bind together before any product leaves
advancedTest.explain: The enzyme is modified to PMP and releases the first keto acid before the second keto acid binds. That is a double-displacement mechanism.

advancedTest.q: In liver zonation, the perivenous glutamine synthetase rim mainly serves to:
choices: Scavenge ammonia that escapes periportal urea synthesis
Make urea when portal ammonia levels are low
Release glutamine into bile for excretion
Supply ammonia to the periportal urea cycle cells
advancedTest.explain: Perivenous glutamine synthetase is a high-affinity, low-capacity backup that captures residual ammonia before blood leaves the liver.

advancedTest.q: In HI/HA syndrome, protein meals provoke hypoglycemia because:
choices: Ammonia from protein directly blocks gluconeogenesis inside the liver
Excess urea synthesis uses up the liver's stored glycogen and glucose
Leucine activates GTP-insensitive GDH, driving beta-cell ATP and insulin
Leucine suppresses glucagon release from pancreatic alpha cells after meals
advancedTest.explain: Mutant GDH escapes GTP inhibition, and leucine activation drives glutamate oxidation, ATP production and insulin secretion.

advancedTest.q: Why does alcohol-associated liver disease often show an AST:ALT ratio above 2?
choices: Alcohol raises AST in skeletal muscle without affecting the liver
ALT is cleared from blood faster when ethanol is present
Alcohol directly stimulates AST gene transcription in the liver
PLP depletion lowers ALT more, with mitochondrial AST release
advancedTest.explain: ALT is more sensitive to PLP deficiency, and mitochondrial injury releases mitochondrial AST, so the ratio rises.

lessons.title: The Urea Cycle and Hyperammonemia

levels.kid:
When your body uses protein for energy, it makes a leftover called **ammonia**. Ammonia is like smoke from a campfire. A little is okay, but too much is harmful, especially to your brain.

Your **liver** is the cleanup crew. It runs a spinning wheel of steps called the **urea cycle**. Each turn of the wheel grabs ammonia and wraps it into a safer package called **urea**.

Urea travels in your blood to your **kidneys**. Then it leaves your body in your pee.

Some babies are born with one broken step in the wheel. Ammonia builds up, and they can get very sleepy and sick. Doctors act fast to clean the blood and give special medicines and food plans.
levels.hs:
Breaking down amino acids releases nitrogen as **ammonia** (NH3, mostly present as ammonium, NH4+, in blood). Ammonia is toxic, especially to the brain, so mammals convert it to **urea**, a small, water-soluble, nontoxic molecule the kidneys excrete. This happens in the **urea cycle**, which runs mainly in liver cells called hepatocytes.

Key ideas:
- Each urea molecule carries **two nitrogen atoms**. One comes from free ammonia, the other from the amino acid **aspartate**.
- The carbon comes from **bicarbonate** (dissolved CO2).
- The cycle costs energy: **4 high-energy phosphate bonds** per urea.
- It spans two compartments. The first steps happen in the **mitochondria** and the rest in the **cytoplasm**.
- **Ornithine** is the carrier molecule. It is regenerated each turn, like a bus that keeps returning to pick up passengers.

When the cycle fails, ammonia rises in the blood. This is called **hyperammonemia**. It causes vomiting, confusion, sleepiness, seizures and, if severe, coma, because ammonia causes brain swelling.

A real example: **ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency** is the most common inherited urea cycle disorder. Its gene sits on the X chromosome, so boys are usually hit hardest. Affected newborns can seem normal at first, then become lethargic within days of starting milk feeds. Adults with severe liver disease (cirrhosis) can also develop hyperammonemia.
levels.college:
The urea cycle, described by **Hans Krebs and Kurt Henseleit in 1932** (the first metabolic cycle discovered), converts ammonia into urea in periportal hepatocytes.

**The five core steps:**
- **Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1)**, mitochondrial: NH4+ + HCO3- + 2 ATP give carbamoyl phosphate. This is the rate-limiting, committed step.
- **Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC)**, mitochondrial: carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine give **citrulline**, which is exported to the cytosol.
- **Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1)**, cytosolic: citrulline + aspartate + ATP give argininosuccinate + AMP + PPi. Hydrolysis of PPi makes this cost 2 phosphate bonds.
- **Argininosuccinate lyase (ASL)**: cleaves argininosuccinate to **arginine + fumarate**.
- **Arginase 1 (ARG1)**: hydrolyzes arginine to **urea + ornithine**. Ornithine re-enters the mitochondria through the ornithine/citrulline transporter **ORNT1** (SLC25A15).

**Overall:** NH4+ + HCO3- + aspartate + 3 ATP give urea + fumarate + 2 ADP + AMP + 2 Pi + PPi, totaling 4 phosphate bonds.

**Regulation:** CPS1 has an absolute requirement for **N-acetylglutamate (NAG)**, made by NAG synthase (NAGS) from acetyl-CoA and glutamate. Arginine activates NAGS, so a protein-rich meal raises NAG and switches on the cycle. Over days, high-protein diets and fasting (via glucagon and glucocorticoids) induce urea cycle enzymes.

**The Krebs bicycle:** fumarate enters the TCA cycle and becomes malate, then oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate can be transaminated back to aspartate, linking the two cycles.

**Hyperammonemia** results from enzyme defects or from liver failure. Lab clues help localize the block:
- High **orotic acid** in urine plus low citrulline points to **OTC deficiency**. Excess carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis.
- Low citrulline without orotic aciduria points to **CPS1 or NAGS deficiency**.
- Very high citrulline points to ASS1 deficiency (**citrullinemia**).
- Argininosuccinic acid in plasma points to ASL deficiency.
- **Arginase deficiency** causes high arginine and progressive spastic diplegia, with milder hyperammonemia.
levels.phd:
**Neurotoxicity of ammonia.** The brain has no urea cycle. It detoxifies ammonia through **glutamine synthetase**, which is located in astrocytes. In hyperammonemia, glutamine accumulates in astrocytes, and this has two effects:
- It draws in water osmotically, causing cytotoxic edema.
- It is shuttled into mitochondria and cleaved back to ammonia (the "**Trojan horse**" hypothesis of Albrecht and Norenberg), driving oxidative stress and the mitochondrial permeability transition.

Other contributors:
- NH4+ substitutes for K+ on transporters, including NKCC1.
- It impairs astrocytic glutamate uptake.
- It depletes α-ketoglutarate by reversing glutamate dehydrogenase flux.
- It increases GABAergic tone, partly through neurosteroids acting on GABA-A receptors.
- It raises brain tryptophan transport via glutamine efflux exchange.

Raised **intracranial pressure**, which can progress to herniation, is the lethal endpoint in neonatal crises and acute liver failure. Arterial ammonia levels correlate with herniation risk in acute liver failure.

**Metabolic architecture.** Häussinger's work showed **hepatic zonation**:
- Periportal hepatocytes run the high-capacity, low-affinity urea cycle.
- A thin rim of perivenous cells expresses high-affinity glutamine synthetase. This rim scavenges ammonia that escapes, giving a sequential low-capacity backup.

Ureagenesis also consumes bicarbonate, so it contributes to systemic acid-base balance. This role is debated, but it means the liver adjusts urea versus glutamine output with pH.

**Enzymology.**
- CPS1 is one of the most abundant mitochondrial matrix proteins, about 15-20% in hepatocytes. It forms carbamoyl phosphate through three sequential phosphorylation and condensation steps, using two ATP.
- NAG binding produces an allosteric conformational change in its C-terminal domain.
- **CPS2** is distinct: cytosolic, glutamine-dependent and part of the CAD trifunctional protein. It feeds pyrimidine synthesis. This explains orotic aciduria in OTC deficiency.
- Supramolecular channeling between CPS1 and OTC on the inner membrane has been proposed but is incompletely established.

**Genetics.** All urea cycle disorders are autosomal recessive except **OTC deficiency (X-linked)**. Owing to lyonization, heterozygous females range from asymptomatic to severe. Symptoms may be unmasked by postpartum catabolism, steroids or valproate. **Valproate** precipitates hyperammonemia by inhibiting CPS1 indirectly. It does this by depleting NAG and sequestering CoA as valproyl-CoA.

**ASL** sits at a node with nitric oxide synthesis. ASL deficiency causes NO deficiency, hypertension and liver disease that persists despite ammonia control. This suggests that complications beyond ammonia arise from loss of the arginine-NO pathway.
levels.expert:
**Recognizing the crisis.** A neonate presenting with lethargy, poor feeding and **respiratory alkalosis** (ammonia stimulates central respiratory drive) is often first treated for sepsis. Measure ammonia in any unexplained encephalopathy. Sample handling matters:
- Use free-flowing blood, ideally without a tourniquet.
- Collect into an EDTA tube, put it on ice, and analyze within about 30 minutes.
- Hemolysis and delay give false elevations.

The differential includes organic acidemias, which cause secondary NAG deficiency through propionyl-CoA and usually produce metabolic acidosis with high anion gap. It also includes fatty acid oxidation defects, transient hyperammonemia of the newborn, portosystemic shunts and hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia syndrome (activating **GLUD1** mutations).

**Acute management principles:**
- Stop protein intake briefly.
- Reverse catabolism with high glucose calories, with or without lipid and insulin.
- Give IV **nitrogen scavengers** (sodium phenylacetate/sodium benzoate). Phenylacetate conjugates glutamine to phenylacetylglutamine; benzoate conjugates glycine to hippurate. Both are excreted in urine, bypassing the cycle.
- Give IV arginine, which becomes semi-essential in most defects. Citrulline is an alternative in OTC and CPS1 deficiency.
- **Carglumic acid**, a stable NAG analogue, essentially cures NAGS deficiency. It also rescues secondary NAG deficiency in propionic and methylmalonic acidemia.
- Severe or refractory levels need urgent **hemodialysis**, preferably high-flow continuous kidney replacement therapy in neonates. Peritoneal dialysis is far less efficient.
- Neurologic outcome tracks peak ammonia and, especially, the duration of coma. This makes speed decisive.

**Chronic care.** Mainstays are a low-protein diet with essential amino acid supplements and oral scavengers. **Glycerol phenylbutyrate** improved tolerability over sodium phenylbutyrate. Valproate should be avoided. **Liver transplantation** corrects hepatic ureagenesis and is offered for severe neonatal-onset disease. It does not reverse prior brain injury. Hepatocyte infusion and auxiliary grafts remain bridging strategies.

**Frontiers and open questions.**
- **Gene therapy**: AAV-mediated OTC gene delivery (for example DTX301) and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle approaches (for example ARCT-810) are in trials.
- A key challenge is AAV episome loss as the infant liver grows.
- Base editing corrected a CPS1 variant in an infant ("baby KJ," reported in 2025). It was the first personalized in vivo CRISPR therapy.
- Hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis shares mechanisms but adds inflammation and gut-derived ammonia. It is treated with lactulose and rifaximin. Ammonia levels correlate poorly with grade in chronic disease, a frequent pitfall.

keyPoints: The urea cycle in the liver converts toxic ammonia into urea for urinary excretion
Urea's two nitrogens come from ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and aspartate
CPS1 is rate-limiting and requires N-acetylglutamate, made by NAGS
The cycle spans mitochondria and cytosol and costs 4 high-energy phosphate bonds
OTC deficiency is X-linked; high orotic acid with low citrulline is its signature
Hyperammonemia swells astrocytes via glutamine, causing brain edema; treatment is urgent

test.q: In which organ does the complete urea cycle mainly run?
test.explain: Hepatocytes run the full urea cycle. The kidneys excrete urea but do not make it from ammonia.

test.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step of the urea cycle?
test.explain: CPS1 makes carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate. It is the committed, regulated step.

test.q: Which molecule supplies the second nitrogen atom of urea?
test.explain: Aspartate donates its nitrogen in the ASS1 step. Ornithine is the recycled carrier, not a nitrogen donor.

test.q: CPS1 requires which allosteric activator?
test.explain: N-acetylglutamate, made by NAGS from acetyl-CoA and glutamate, is absolutely required for CPS1 activity.

test.q: Which urea cycle step releases fumarate that links to the TCA cycle?
test.explain: ASL cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate, forming the 'Krebs bicycle' link.

test.q: A boy has high ammonia, low citrulline and high urinary orotic acid. The likely defect is in:
test.explain: In OTC deficiency, excess carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, producing orotic acid. CPS1 deficiency lowers citrulline without orotic aciduria.

test.q: Why does OTC deficiency usually affect males more severely?
choices: The OTC gene is on the X chromosome
test.explain: OTC deficiency is X-linked, so males with one faulty copy are affected. Females are mosaic because of X-inactivation.

test.q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds are used to make one urea?
test.explain: Three ATP are used, but one is split to AMP plus PPi. PPi hydrolysis adds a bond, so the total is four.

test.q: In the brain, ammonia is detoxified mainly by which astrocyte enzyme?
test.explain: The brain lacks a urea cycle. Astrocytic glutamine synthetase makes glutamine, whose buildup causes swelling.

test.q: Elevated ammonia in the blood is called ___.
test.explain: Hyperammonemia causes vomiting, confusion, seizures and brain edema.

test.q: Which amino acid is the recycled carrier of the urea cycle, re-entering the mitochondria each turn?
test.explain: Arginase releases ornithine with urea, and ORNT1 transports it back into the mitochondria.

test.q: Arginase splits arginine into urea and ___.
test.explain: Arginase regenerates ornithine, closing the cycle.

kidTest.q: What harmful leftover do our bodies make when they use protein?
kidTest.explain: Using protein makes ammonia, which is harmful in large amounts.

kidTest.q: Which organ runs the urea cycle wheel?
kidTest.explain: The liver is the cleanup crew that turns ammonia into urea.

kidTest.q: How does urea leave the body?
kidTest.explain: The kidneys send urea out in urine.

kidTest.q: Which body part is hurt most by too much ammonia?
kidTest.explain: Too much ammonia makes the brain swell, causing sleepiness and illness.

kidTest.q: The liver wraps ammonia into a safer package called u _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Urea is the safer package that leaves in urine.

advancedTest.q: A patient has hyperammonemia with very low citrulline but normal urinary orotic acid. The most consistent defect is:
advancedTest.explain: Without carbamoyl phosphate there is no spillover into orotic acid, and citrulline stays low. OTC deficiency would raise orotic acid.

advancedTest.q: Why does carglumic acid help some propionic acidemia patients with hyperammonemia?
choices: It conjugates glycine into hippurate for urinary loss
It directly inhibits glutamine synthetase in astrocytes
It replaces deficient NAG and reactivates CPS1
It supplies arginine to restart the cycle downstream
advancedTest.explain: Propionyl-CoA causes secondary NAG deficiency. Carglumic acid is a stable NAG analogue that reactivates CPS1. Benzoate, not carglumic acid, makes hippurate.

advancedTest.q: In the 'Trojan horse' hypothesis, ammonia damages astrocytes mainly because:
choices: Ornithine accumulates and blocks potassium channels
Urea crosses into neurons and denatures proteins
Glutamine enters mitochondria and is cleaved back to ammonia
Fumarate depletes and halts the TCA cycle in neurons
advancedTest.explain: Glutamine made by astrocytes is carried into mitochondria and cleaved back to ammonia, driving oxidative stress and permeability transition.

advancedTest.q: ASL-deficient patients develop hypertension despite good ammonia control. The best explanation is:
choices: Loss of the arginine-nitric oxide pathway
Excess urea production raises plasma osmolality
advancedTest.explain: ASL also channels arginine to nitric oxide synthesis. Its loss causes NO deficiency independent of ammonia.

lessons.title: From Amino Acids to Neurotransmitters: Catecholamines, Serotonin and GABA

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk to each other with tiny chemical messages. Many of these messages are made from **amino acids**, the same building blocks found in the protein you eat.

Think of a kitchen. An amino acid is the raw ingredient. Special helpers called **enzymes** are the cooks. They chop and change the ingredient, step by step, into a finished dish: a brain message.

- From one ingredient, cooks make **dopamine**, which helps you move and feel rewarded.
- From another, they make **serotonin**, which helps with mood and sleep.
- From a third, they make **GABA**, which tells busy brain cells to calm down.

If a cook is missing, the dish does not get made, and the body can get sick.
levels.hs:
A **neurotransmitter** is a chemical that a nerve cell releases to pass a signal to another cell. Several of the most important ones are built from amino acids in just a few enzyme steps.

**Catecholamines** come from the amino acid **tyrosine**, which your body can also make from **phenylalanine**. The steps run: tyrosine → L-DOPA → **dopamine** → **norepinephrine** → **epinephrine** (adrenaline). Dopamine matters for movement and reward. Norepinephrine and epinephrine drive the "fight or flight" response.

**Serotonin** comes from **tryptophan**, an essential amino acid you must get from food. Serotonin helps regulate mood, sleep, appetite and gut movement. Most of the body's serotonin is actually made in the gut, not the brain.

**GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is made from **glutamate**. This is a striking switch, because glutamate is the brain's main "go" (excitatory) signal, while GABA is the main "stop" (inhibitory) signal. One enzyme step turns an accelerator into a brake.

Real example: in **Parkinson's disease**, dopamine-making neurons die. Dopamine itself can't cross into the brain from the blood, so doctors give its precursor, **L-DOPA (levodopa)**. The brain's enzymes then convert it into dopamine, partly restoring movement.
levels.college:
Neurotransmitter synthesis reuses ordinary amino acid chemistry: hydroxylations, decarboxylations and methylations, each catalyzed by a specific enzyme with a specific cofactor.

**Catecholamine pathway** (in the cytosol, except one step):
- Tyrosine → L-DOPA by **tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)**, which uses O2, Fe²⁺ and **tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)**. This is the **rate-limiting step**.
- L-DOPA → dopamine by **aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC)**, which needs **pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6)**.
- Dopamine → norepinephrine by **dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH)**, a copper enzyme that uses **ascorbate (vitamin C)**. It works *inside* synaptic vesicles.
- Norepinephrine → epinephrine by **PNMT**, using **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)** as the methyl donor. PNMT is concentrated in the adrenal medulla and is induced by cortisol.

**Serotonin pathway**:
- Tryptophan → 5-hydroxytryptophan by **tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH)**, which is BH4-dependent and rate-limiting. TPH1 works in gut enterochromaffin cells and the pineal gland; TPH2 works in brain raphe neurons.
- 5-HTP → serotonin (5-HT) by the same AADC (PLP).
- In the pineal gland, serotonin → **melatonin** via N-acetylation and O-methylation.

**GABA**: glutamate → GABA by **glutamate decarboxylase (GAD)**, which is PLP-dependent. GABA is cleared by GABA transaminase (also PLP) to succinic semialdehyde, which then enters the TCA cycle as succinate. This loop is called the **GABA shunt**.

**Inactivation** of monoamines: reuptake transporters (DAT, NET, SERT) recycle them. **Monoamine oxidase (MAO)**, a mitochondrial enzyme, and **catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)** degrade them. The main end products are **HVA** (from dopamine), **VMA** (from norepinephrine and epinephrine) and **5-HIAA** (from serotonin), all measurable in urine.

Clinical link: untreated **phenylketonuria** (no phenylalanine hydroxylase, which is also BH4-dependent) lowers tyrosine and catecholamine supply. Vitamin B6 deficiency lowers GABA, which can cause seizures.
levels.phd:
**Regulation of tyrosine hydroxylase.** TH sets the pace of catecholamine output. Short-term control comes from feedback inhibition: catecholamines chelate the active-site Fe³⁺ and compete with BH4. This feedback is relieved by phosphorylation of the regulatory domain. PKA phosphorylates Ser40, the key activating site; Ser19 phosphorylation by CaMKII recruits 14-3-3 proteins; Ser31 is phosphorylated by ERK. Long-term control comes from induction of TH transcription, for example during sustained sympathetic activity. Nagatsu, Levitt and Udenfriend identified TH as the rate-limiting step in 1964.

**BH4 as a shared bottleneck.** Phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases all depend on BH4. BH4 is made from GTP by GTP cyclohydrolase I (GTPCH), then 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase. It is recycled by pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase and dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR). Dominant GTPCH1 mutations cause **Segawa dopa-responsive dystonia**, which responds dramatically to levodopa. Recessive BH4 defects cause hyperphenylalaninemia plus combined dopamine and serotonin deficiency, which dietary phenylalanine restriction alone does not correct.

**Compartmentation.** VMAT2 loads cytosolic dopamine into vesicles using a proton gradient set up by the V-ATPase. Inside the vesicle, membrane-bound and soluble DBH convert dopamine to norepinephrine using ascorbate, which is regenerated from cytochrome b561 via semidehydroascorbate. PNMT in the adrenal medulla depends on cortisol arriving through the intra-adrenal portal circulation. This is a classic example of anatomy shaping biochemistry.

**Tryptophan competition.** Brain serotonin synthesis is substrate-sensitive because TPH2 is not saturated at physiological tryptophan levels. Tryptophan competes with other large neutral amino acids for LAT1 transport across the blood-brain barrier. Fernstrom and Wurtman's 1970s studies of the plasma tryptophan:LNAA ratio linked diet to brain 5-HT, though the behavioral effects of this remain debated. About 95% of tryptophan is actually catabolized by the **kynurenine pathway** (IDO/TDO). Inflammation induces IDO, which diverts tryptophan away from serotonin and produces neuroactive kynurenic and quinolinic acids.

**GAD isoforms.** GAD67 is constitutively active and produces most cytosolic GABA. GAD65 binds to vesicles, exists mostly as PLP-free apoenzyme, and supplies GABA on demand. GAD65 is the major autoantigen in stiff-person syndrome and type 1 diabetes.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostics.** Neurotransmitter disorders are diagnosed mainly from CSF, because urinary metabolites largely reflect peripheral turnover. A CSF panel measures HVA, 5-HIAA, 3-O-methyldopa (3-OMD), pterins and 5-MTHF. Pre-analytic pitfalls are real: there is a rostrocaudal gradient, so a standardized fraction must be collected; samples must be frozen at the bedside and protected from light; and blood contamination degrades the results. Reading the patterns:
- Low HVA with normal 5-HIAA suggests TH deficiency.
- Low HVA and low 5-HIAA with high 3-OMD suggests **AADC deficiency**. Plasma AADC activity and a dried-blood-spot 3-OMD newborn screen help confirm it.
- Abnormal pterins identify BH4 defects.

**Gene therapy milestone.** AADC deficiency causes oculogyric crises and severe hypotonia, and many children never achieve head control. **Eladocagene exuparvovec** (Upstaza/Kebilidi) delivers *DDC* by AAV2 through stereotactic, MRI-guided bilateral putaminal infusion. It was approved in the EU in 2022 and by the FDA in 2024, using an image-guided delivery approach that is directly relevant to neurosurgery. PET imaging with 18F-DOPA showed new putaminal dopamine synthesis, and treated children gained motor milestones.

**Pharmacologic logic, mechanisms only.** Levodopa is paired with peripheral AADC inhibitors (carbidopa, benserazide), and often with COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone) or MAO-B inhibitors, to protect the precursor's supply to the brain. Metyrosine inhibits TH and is used in pheochromocytoma. Telotristat inhibits peripheral TPH1 and reduces carcinoid diarrhea. Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase; it is useful in infantile spasms but carries a risk of retinal toxicity. MAO inhibitors combined with dietary tyramine can cause a hypertensive crisis. Excess serotonergic drug combinations risk serotonin syndrome.

**Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy** (*ALDH7A1*) is caused by an accumulating metabolite, P6C, that inactivates PLP, which starves GAD. It presents as refractory neonatal seizures that respond to B6. Elevated α-aminoadipic semialdehyde is the biomarker.

**Open questions** include:
- the relative roles of gut-derived versus central serotonin in mood and in the gut-brain axis;
- the dysregulation of TH phosphorylation in Parkinson's disease;
- whether neurotoxic dopamine metabolites, especially DOPAL formed by MAO, drive the vulnerability of nigral neurons;
- how inflammation-driven kynurenine shunting contributes to depression.

AADC (vitamin B6/PLP) makes both dopamine and serotonin

Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier where dopamine does not

lessons.title: One-Carbon Metabolism: Folate, B12 and Methylation

levels.kid:
Your body builds things all day long, like new blood cells and new DNA. To do that, it needs tiny building pieces made of just **one carbon** atom.

Two vitamins act like delivery trucks for these pieces. One is **folate**, found in leafy green vegetables and beans. The other is **vitamin B12**, found in meat, eggs and milk.

The trucks carry one-carbon pieces to where they are needed. One special piece, called a **methyl group**, works like a sticky note. Cells stick it onto DNA to mark which genes to use.

If the trucks stop running, the body can't make new blood cells properly. They come out too big and too few. That's why doctors check these vitamins.
levels.hs:
**One-carbon metabolism** is a set of reactions that move single-carbon units (like methyl, -CH3, or formyl, -CHO groups) between molecules. These units are needed to build DNA and to add chemical tags to many molecules.

The key carrier is **folate** (vitamin B9). Inside cells it becomes **tetrahydrofolate (THF)**, which picks up a carbon unit, often from the amino acid **serine**, and hands it off for:
- Making **thymidine** and **purines**, the building blocks of DNA
- Recycling the amino acid **homocysteine** back into **methionine**

That last step needs **vitamin B12** too. Methionine is then turned into **SAM (S-adenosylmethionine)**, the cell's main methyl donor. SAM puts methyl groups on DNA, proteins and neurotransmitters. After donating, SAM becomes homocysteine again, closing the loop.

When folate or B12 is low, cells that divide fast, like bone marrow, can't copy DNA properly. The result is **megaloblastic anemia**: large, immature red blood cells. B12 deficiency can also damage nerves.

Real example: many countries add folic acid to flour because low folate early in pregnancy raises the risk of **neural tube defects** like spina bifida. After the US began fortification in 1998, these birth defects fell by roughly a quarter or more.

Some cancer drugs, like **methotrexate**, work by blocking folate use, starving fast-dividing cancer cells of DNA building blocks.
levels.college:
One-carbon (1C) metabolism links folate, the methionine cycle and nucleotide synthesis.

**The folate cycle.** Dietary folate and synthetic folic acid are reduced by **dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)** to **tetrahydrofolate (THF)**. **Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT)** transfers serine's side-chain carbon to THF, producing glycine and **5,10-methylene-THF**. This hub carbon has three fates:
- **Thymidylate synthase** methylates dUMP to dTMP, oxidizing the folate to DHF, which DHFR must regenerate.
- Oxidation to 10-formyl-THF, which donates carbons C2 and C8 of the purine ring.
- Irreversible reduction by **MTHFR** to **5-methyl-THF**.

**The methionine cycle.** **Methionine synthase** moves the methyl from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine, forming methionine. Its cofactor is **methylcobalamin** (B12). Methionine adenosyltransferase makes **SAM**, which donates methyl groups through methyltransferases (DNMTs, histone methyltransferases, COMT, PNMT), leaving **SAH**. SAH is hydrolyzed to homocysteine. Homocysteine can also be remethylated by betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase in the liver, or channeled by **cystathionine beta-synthase** (B6-dependent) into cysteine via transsulfuration.

**B12's second job.** Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for **methylmalonyl-CoA mutase**, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. So B12 deficiency raises both **homocysteine** and **methylmalonic acid (MMA)**. Folate deficiency raises only homocysteine.

**The methyl trap.** Without B12, folate accumulates as 5-methyl-THF, which can't be converted back. Functional folate deficiency follows, causing megaloblastic anemia even with adequate folate intake.

**Drugs.** Methotrexate inhibits DHFR. Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR. 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase.
levels.phd:
Modern 1C metabolism is compartmentalized. In proliferating cells, most serine-derived 1C units come from **mitochondria**: SHMT2 cleaves serine, and MTHFD2 (with MTHFD1L) oxidizes methylene-THF to **formate**, which exits to the cytosol. There, trifunctional MTHFD1 reloads formate onto THF for purine and thymidylate synthesis. Mitochondrial 1C flux also generates NADPH and supports formylation of initiator methionyl-tRNA (fMet-tRNA) for mitochondrial translation. **MTHFD2** is among the most consistently overexpressed metabolic enzymes across tumors and is nearly absent in most adult tissues, making it an attractive drug target.

**Regulation.** SAM allosterically inhibits MTHFR and activates CBS. High SAM therefore diverts homocysteine toward transsulfuration, and low SAM favors remethylation. **Glycine N-methyltransferase** buffers hepatic SAM by methylating glycine to sarcosine. The **SAM/SAH ratio** is often called the methylation index, since SAH is a potent product inhibitor of most methyltransferases. SAH hydrolase equilibrium actually favors SAH synthesis, so adenosine and homocysteine must be continuously removed.

**Methionine synthase chemistry.** Cob(I)alamin is a supernucleophile that takes the methyl from 5-methyl-THF, then transfers it to homocysteine. Occasional oxidation to cob(II)alamin inactivates the enzyme. **Methionine synthase reductase** reactivates it using SAM as the methyl source. Nitrous oxide oxidizes cob(I)alamin irreversibly, which explains anesthesia-associated myelopathy in B12-deficient patients.

**Classic work.** Herbert's 1962 self-experiment on a folate-free diet charted the sequence of deficiency: low serum folate, then hypersegmented neutrophils, then megaloblastosis. The MRC Vitamin Study (1991) proved periconceptional folic acid prevents most recurrent neural tube defects.

**Controversies.** The common **MTHFR C677T** variant makes a thermolabile enzyme that raises homocysteine, mainly when folate is low. However, its links to cardiovascular disease and pregnancy loss have largely not held up. Lowering homocysteine with B vitamins in trials such as HOPE-2 and NORVIT did not reduce cardiovascular events. Homocysteine thus appears to be a risk marker more than a cause. Why B12 deficiency demyelinates nerves (impaired methylation versus odd-chain fatty acid buildup from MMA) remains unresolved.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the key distinction is **B12 versus folate deficiency**, because giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient can correct the anemia while **subacute combined degeneration** progresses. This involves the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Neurological injury can occur with normal hemoglobin and normal MCV. Serum B12 is insensitive near the low-normal range, so **MMA** and homocysteine serve as functional tests. MMA is specific for B12 but rises in renal failure. Holotranscobalamin is an earlier marker. Causes to consider include pernicious anemia (anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies), metformin, long-term proton pump inhibitors, ileal resection, vegan diets and bariatric surgery.

**Neurosurgical and anesthetic pitfalls.** Nitrous oxide exposure can unmask latent B12 deficiency, producing myeloneuropathy after surgery. On MRI this shows as the dorsal-column "inverted V" T2 signal, which can mimic compressive or inflammatory cord disease. The same pattern is increasingly seen in nitrous oxide toxicity presentations. Antiepileptics such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and valproate perturb folate metabolism, which matters for teratogenic risk counselling in women with epilepsy.

**Pharmacology.** High-dose methotrexate regimens use **leucovorin** (folinic acid) rescue. Leucovorin bypasses DHFR, so it repletes reduced folate in normal tissues. **Glucarpidase** cleaves methotrexate in renal failure. Pemetrexed requires folate and B12 premedication to reduce marrow and mucosal toxicity. Leucovorin also *potentiates* 5-FU by stabilizing the ternary complex of 5-FdUMP, thymidylate synthase and methylene-THF. **Cerebral folate deficiency**, often due to autoantibodies against folate receptor alpha, causes low CSF 5-methyl-THF despite normal serum folate. It responds to folinic acid, which is being explored in subsets of autism.

**Inborn errors.** Classical homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) causes lens dislocation, marfanoid habitus and thrombosis. Some patients respond to B6, and betaine helps others. **CblC disease** causes combined methylmalonic aciduria with homocystinuria.

**Frontiers.** Inhibitors of SHMT and MTHFD2 are in development. MAT2A inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality in **MTAP-deleted** cancers, including some gliomas. Dietary methionine restriction is being studied as a way to sensitize tumors to therapy. Open questions include how much SAM fluctuation actually reprograms the epigenome in vivo, and whether unmetabolized folic acid from fortification has biological effects.

keyPoints: Folate (as THF) carries one-carbon units, mostly from serine, for building DNA
Methylene-THF feeds thymidylate (dTMP) and purine synthesis
Methionine synthase uses B12 to remethylate homocysteine to methionine
SAM is the universal methyl donor; it becomes SAH, then homocysteine
B12 deficiency raises homocysteine AND methylmalonic acid; folate deficiency raises only homocysteine
Methotrexate, trimethoprim and 5-FU work by blocking folate-dependent enzymes

lessons.title: Purine and Pyrimidine Synthesis, Salvage and Breakdown

levels.kid:
Your DNA is written with four letters: A, G, C and T. Each letter is a small molecule called a **nucleotide**. Your cells need lots of them, especially when they grow and divide.

The letters come in two families. **Purines** (A and G) are big, with two rings, like a pair of glasses. **Pyrimidines** (C, T and U) are smaller, with one ring.

Cells can build these letters from scratch, a bit like baking bread from flour. They can also **recycle** old letters, like reusing LEGO bricks instead of buying new ones. Recycling saves a lot of energy.

When purines are finally thrown away, they become **uric acid**. If too much uric acid builds up, it can form sharp crystals in a toe. That painful problem is called gout.
levels.hs:
**Nucleotides** are the building blocks of DNA and RNA. They also make energy carriers like ATP and GTP. Each nucleotide has a nitrogen-containing **base**, a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), and one or more phosphates.

The bases come in two families:
- **Purines** have two fused rings: adenine (A) and guanine (G).
- **Pyrimidines** have one ring: cytosine (C), thymine (T, DNA only) and uracil (U, RNA only).

Cells get nucleotides in two ways:
- **De novo synthesis** ("from new"): the base is built step by step from small pieces. These pieces include amino acids (glycine, glutamine, aspartate), CO2 and folate-carried carbons. This takes a lot of ATP.
- **Salvage**: recycling bases freed when DNA and RNA are broken down. This is much cheaper.

Both routes start from an activated sugar called **PRPP** (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate).

Breakdown differs by family. Purines are turned into **uric acid**, which humans cannot break down further. Pyrimidines are broken into small, water-soluble molecules that are easy to get rid of.

A real example: **gout**. When uric acid levels in the blood get too high, needle-shaped crystals form in joints, often the big toe. The drug **allopurinol** treats gout by blocking **xanthine oxidase**, the enzyme that makes uric acid.
levels.college:
**Purine de novo synthesis** builds the ring directly on ribose-5-phosphate. PRPP, made by **PRPP synthetase**, is the starting point.
- The committed step is **glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase**, which yields 5-phosphoribosylamine.
- Ring atoms come from glycine (C4, C5, N7), glutamine (N3, N9), aspartate (N1), CO2 (C6) and two **N10-formyl-THF** carbons (C2, C8).
- About ten steps produce **IMP** (inosine monophosphate). IMP branches to AMP using aspartate and GTP, or to GMP using glutamine and ATP. This cross-use of energy balances the two pools.
- AMP, GMP and IMP feed back to inhibit the amidotransferase. PRPP activates it.

**Pyrimidine de novo synthesis** builds the ring first and then attaches it to PRPP.
- **CAD**, a single protein with three enzyme activities (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, aspartate transcarbamoylase, dihydroorotase), makes dihydroorotate. CPS II is cytosolic and uses glutamine, unlike the mitochondrial CPS I of the urea cycle.
- **Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase** (on the inner mitochondrial membrane) makes orotate.
- **UMP synthase** adds PRPP and decarboxylates to give UMP. UMP becomes UTP, then CTP via CTP synthetase.

**Deoxyribonucleotides** come from **ribonucleotide reductase** (RNR), which reduces NDPs to dNDPs. **Thymidylate synthase** methylates dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylene-THF. **Dihydrofolate reductase** (DHFR) then regenerates THF.

**Salvage**: **HGPRT** converts hypoxanthine and guanine to IMP and GMP. **APRT** converts adenine to AMP.

**Breakdown**: purines go to hypoxanthine and then xanthine, and xanthine oxidase converts xanthine to uric acid. Pyrimidines are degraded to β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate.
levels.phd:
**Regulation** is dense and logically coupled.
- **Purine branch**: the amidotransferase shows concerted inhibition by adenine and guanine nucleotides. PRPP availability is often rate-limiting, which is why gain-of-function **PRPS1** mutations cause purine overproduction and gout.
- **Pyrimidine branch**: in mammals, CPS II is activated by PRPP and ATP and inhibited by UTP. In *E. coli*, the classic allosteric model enzyme is ATCase, inhibited by CTP and activated by ATP. Gerhart and Pardee's ATCase work founded the field of allostery.
- **mTORC1 and growth signaling**: S6K1 phosphorylates CAD to drive pyrimidine flux. mTORC1 also induces MTHFD2 through ATF4, supplying one-carbon units for purine synthesis.

**Ribonucleotide reductase** uses a radical mechanism. The class Ia enzyme has α2 (R1) and β2 (R2) subunits. A tyrosyl radical, generated by a di-iron centre in R2, is passed over about 35 Å through a proton-coupled electron-transfer pathway to a cysteine thiyl radical in R1.

Two allosteric sites control RNR:
- **Activity site**: ATP activates the enzyme, while dATP inactivates it by forming α6 rings.
- **Specificity site**: dATP or ATP favours reduction of CDP and UDP. dTTP favours GDP. dGTP favours ADP.

This cross-talk keeps the four dNTP pools balanced. An imbalance is mutagenic.

**Purinosomes**: Benkovic's group showed that the six purine enzymes reversibly cluster near mitochondria when purines are scarce. Whether this channels intermediates is still debated, as are imaging artifacts from overexpressed tagged enzymes.

**Uric acid and evolution**: humans and other apes lost **urate oxidase** (uricase) through pseudogenizing mutations. Proposed benefits include urate's antioxidant capacity and blood pressure maintenance during low-salt diets. Both ideas are plausible but unproven. Plasma urate is set mostly by renal handling, through reabsorption by URAT1 (SLC22A12) and GLUT9 (SLC2A9) and secretion by ABCG2. ABCG2 Q141K is a major gout-risk variant.

Thymidylate synthase forms a covalent ternary complex with substrate and cofactor. **FdUMP**, the active metabolite of 5-fluorouracil, traps this complex as a classic suicide inhibitor.
levels.expert:
Nucleotide pathways are among the most heavily drugged in medicine. Their failures produce distinctive syndromes.

**Pharmacology by target:**
- **Methotrexate** blocks DHFR. **Pemetrexed** inhibits TS, DHFR and GARFT. **5-FU and capecitabine** act on TS. **Hydroxyurea** quenches the RNR tyrosyl radical. **Gemcitabine** inactivates RNR and is incorporated into DNA, where it causes masked chain termination.
- **Mycophenolate** inhibits IMPDH, and lymphocytes depend heavily on de novo guanine synthesis. **Leflunomide/teriflunomide** inhibit DHODH, which is the rationale in MS and rheumatoid arthritis. **Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine** need HGPRT activation and are inactivated by TPMT and xanthine oxidase. Combining them with allopurinol or febuxostat without adjustment risks fatal myelosuppression. Pre-treatment TPMT and NUDT15 genotyping is standard practice.
- **Fluoropyrimidines**: deficiency of DPD (DPYD variants), the rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine breakdown, causes severe 5-FU toxicity. Pre-emptive DPYD testing is now recommended by EMA and was added to US labeling in 2024.
- **Hyperuricemia**: **rasburicase**, a recombinant uricase, is used for tumour lysis syndrome. It is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because H2O2 produced by the reaction triggers hemolysis.

**Inborn errors:**
- **Lesch-Nyhan syndrome** (X-linked, near-complete HGPRT loss) causes urate overproduction, dystonia and compulsive self-injury. Basal ganglia dopamine deficits are documented, but the link from purine loss to the neurological picture remains unexplained. Allopurinol fixes the uric acid but not the neurology.
- **ADA deficiency** lets dATP accumulate, which inhibits RNR and destroys lymphocytes, causing SCID. Treatments include PEG-ADA, transplant, and lentiviral gene therapy. **Strimvelis**, a gammaretroviral product, was the first ex vivo gene therapy approved in Europe.
- **Hereditary orotic aciduria** (UMP synthase deficiency) causes megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to B12 or folate but responds to uridine triacetate. The key distinction is that urea-cycle OTC deficiency also raises orotate, but with hyperammonemia.
- **SAMHD1 and RRM2B** mutations unbalance dNTP pools, causing Aicardi-Goutières syndrome and mitochondrial DNA depletion, respectively.

**Open questions**: whether DHODH inhibitors gain traction in AML differentiation therapy; whether purinosome assembly matters in vivo; and whether lowering urate protects the kidney and heart. The CKD-FIX trial found no renal benefit.

keyPoints: Purines (A, G) have two rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one
Both de novo synthesis and salvage start from PRPP
Purine rings are built on ribose to make IMP; pyrimidine rings are built first, then attached
Ribonucleotide reductase makes deoxyribonucleotides; thymidylate synthase makes dTMP
HGPRT salvages purines; its loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
Purines are degraded to uric acid by xanthine oxidase, the target of allopurinol

test.q: Which bases are purines?
test.explain: Purines, adenine and guanine, have two fused rings. The other pairs are one-ring pyrimidines.

test.q: What activated sugar starts both de novo synthesis and salvage of nucleotides?
test.explain: PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) donates the ribose-phosphate in both routes.

test.q: The first complete purine nucleotide made de novo, which then branches to AMP and GMP, is:
test.explain: IMP (inosine monophosphate) is the branch point. UMP and OMP belong to pyrimidine synthesis.

test.q: How does pyrimidine synthesis differ from purine synthesis?
choices: Its ring is built first, then attached to PRPP
It uses no amino acids as building blocks
It takes place inside the cell nucleus
Its ring is built directly on ribose-5-phosphate
test.explain: Pyrimidines form orotate first and then attach it to PRPP. Purines are assembled on the sugar from the start.

test.q: Which enzyme converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides?
test.explain: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces NDPs to dNDPs. Thymidylate synthase only makes dTMP from dUMP.

test.q: Allopurinol lowers uric acid by inhibiting:
test.explain: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Humans lack functional uricase.

test.q: Why do purine and pyrimidine breakdown products cause different problems?
choices: Both form uric acid at equal rates
Purines are broken down to soluble β-alanine
Pyrimidines form uric acid, which crystallizes
Purines form uric acid; pyrimidine products are soluble
test.explain: Purines end as poorly soluble uric acid, which can cause gout. Pyrimidines yield soluble β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate.

test.q: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II differs from CPS I in that CPS II:
choices: Feeds carbamoyl phosphate into the urea cycle
Works in the cytosol and uses glutamine
test.explain: CPS II, part of CAD, is cytosolic and uses glutamine for pyrimidine synthesis. The other options describe CPS I.

test.q: Which cofactor donates the methyl group when thymidylate synthase makes dTMP?
test.explain: Methylene-THF supplies the carbon and is oxidized to DHF, which DHFR then recycles.

test.q: Which salvage enzyme recycles hypoxanthine and guanine? (abbreviation)
test.explain: HGPRT attaches these bases to PRPP to make IMP and GMP.

test.q: High blood uric acid can form crystals in joints, causing the disease ___.
test.explain: Gout often affects the big toe.

test.q: Building nucleotides from small precursors rather than recycling is called de ___ synthesis.
test.explain: De novo means "from new"; salvage is the recycling route.

kidTest.q: What are A, G, C and T in DNA?
kidTest.explain: They are nucleotides, the letters of DNA.

kidTest.q: How are purines different from pyrimidines?
kidTest.explain: Purines are big, with two rings. Pyrimidines have one.

kidTest.q: Why do cells recycle old letters?
kidTest.explain: Recycling is cheaper than building from scratch.

kidTest.q: What can too much uric acid form in a toe?
kidTest.explain: Uric acid crystals cause gout.

kidTest.q: The painful toe problem from uric acid is called g _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Gout comes from uric acid crystals.

advancedTest.q: Why does ADA deficiency cause severe combined immunodeficiency?
choices: Uric acid crystals destroy the thymus during early childhood
Lack of PRPP prevents RNA synthesis in most white cells
Excess dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase in lymphocytes
Excess orotate blocks thymidylate synthase in T cells
advancedTest.explain: dATP binds the activity site of RNR and shuts down dNTP supply, which lymphocytes need to divide.

advancedTest.q: A patient on azathioprine starts allopurinol and develops profound marrow suppression. The best explanation is:
choices: Allopurinol induces TPMT, which creates toxic metabolites
Allopurinol blocks the HGPRT activation step of the drug
6-MP is shunted into active thioguanine nucleotides
Uric acid depletion directly suppresses marrow stem cells
advancedTest.explain: Xanthine oxidase inactivates 6-MP. Blocking it shunts more drug into active cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides.

advancedTest.q: Megaloblastic anemia, high urinary orotate and normal ammonia that respond to uridine but not B12 point to:
advancedTest.explain: These findings fit hereditary orotic aciduria, caused by UMP synthase deficiency. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency would raise ammonia. Folate-related causes would respond to folate replacement and would not raise orotate.

advancedTest.q: Why is rasburicase contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
choices: It depletes the PRPP needed for red blood cell repair
Its reaction makes H2O2, which overwhelms red cells
It raises xanthine, which then precipitates in the kidneys
It directly inhibits the G6PD enzyme inside red cells
advancedTest.explain: The reaction generates hydrogen peroxide. G6PD-deficient cells lack the NADPH needed to neutralize it, so they hemolyze.
